title: She Cried Out for Women's Rights, Yet Was Executed for Treason
dek: Olympe de Gouges is known for her Declaration of the Rights of Woman, but her death was not due to her feminist advocacy, but rather her opposition to the king's execution and her attacks on Robespierre.
why: To understand the political situation and personal fate of women during the French Revolution. History enthusiasts and those interested in feminist issues will find it compelling.
who: Those interested in the French Revolution, women's history, and women's writing during the Enlightenment, especially readers who want to learn about women's political participation beyond what textbooks cover.
skip: The first 4-plus minutes, which cover the ambiguities of her early life, can be fast-forwarded; the core content begins in the middle.

points.h: The Declaration of the Rights of Woman answered the Declaration of the Rights of Man
points.body: Olympe de Gouges is best known for her 1791 Declaration of the Rights of Woman and the Female Citizen, a direct response to the 1789 Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen. The original used citoyen; she changed it to the feminine form citoyenne, which looks quite different but sounds similar. Her writing and political activity went far beyond this pamphlet, and her execution was not for advocating women's rights.

points.h: Biographical truth is mixed with fiction
points.body: The first English biography of de Gouges, Women's Rights in the French Revolution, draws heavily on her epistolary novel Memoirs of Madame de Valmont as factual evidence, but that book is highly fictional. The protagonist is widely considered to be her own stand-in, while the Marquis de Flaucour represents her possible biological father, the Marquis de Pompignan. This lineage remains unconfirmed to this day.

Zamore and Mirza was written in 1784 and submitted anonymously; it was accepted the following year but delayed in production. After de Gouges repeatedly pressed for its staging, the theater revoked her admission privileges and sought her arrest. Between 1761 and 1789, the theater accepted only nine plays by women, and she was the only one treated this way. She later wrote to the Duke of Richelieu, who helped restore her standing.

points.h: The Slavery play became the first abolitionist drama
points.body: When the play finally premiered in 1789, the setting had been changed from the East Indies to the Caribbean, and the characters from Asians to Africans, with the title changed to The Slavery of Blacks. It is often regarded as the first French play explicitly supporting abolition and told from the perspective of the enslaved. Abolitionists praised it, while wealthy colonists hired hecklers to disrupt performances, and actors refused to darken their skin for the roles.

points.h: The article rewrote all 17 articles one by one
points.body: The Declaration of the Rights of Man granted civil rights but excluded women, and the 1791 Constitution restricted voting rights to male taxpayers. De Gouges's Declaration of the Rights of Woman copied the format of the 17 articles, rewriting each one. For example, where the original Article 10 guaranteed freedom of speech, she added that mothers had the right to publicly name the father of their children. The entire work was dedicated to Marie Antoinette, urging her to advance women's rights.

points.h: Defending Louis XVI became a liability
points.body: Despite her revolutionary stance, de Gouges believed constitutional monarchy was best for France, and that the king should be a symbol rather than a power. When Louis XVI was tried for treason in 1792, she voluntarily defended him, arguing that since the monarchy had been abolished, the Republic could not judge the king for actions taken while he was in office. Her logic was criticized as far-fetched; the king was ultimately executed, and she herself was seen as a royalist.

points.h: Her federalist proposal led to her arrest
points.body: In July 1793, de Gouges suggested that French provinces should govern themselves rather than form a unified republic, which was seen as a direct provocation. She underestimated the intense political climate of the Reign of Terror, and voluntarily brought investigators to her office, believing her works would prove her loyalty. Instead, her unfinished play France Preserved, which sympathized with Marie Antoinette, was used as evidence against her. She was ultimately executed on charges of opposing the republican constitution.
